Lessons.Title: Compare Fractions with the Same Denominator
ExplanationParagraphs: The 2021 original warm-up Notice and Wonder: Two More Strips uses ONE partly-covered source photograph/diagram. Both strips use same-size unit-fraction pieces; parts of the second are hidden. Students may have multiple mathematical observations and inferences; do NOT infer an exact hidden count from an obscured photograph or invent a numeric answer. Teacher checks number of visible fractional parts, same whole and reasoning.

Activity1 requires TWO original circle-the-greater pairs: 1/2 versus3/2: the greater is 3/2 (more half-lengths, exceeds one); 3/8 versus2/8: the greater is 3/8. Then FOUR original inequality comparisons: 1/6<4/6;4/4<5/4;2/3>1/3;4/8<6/8. All must be preserved individually with the exact source fractions; equality is NOT an acceptable relation for any of these six.

The original optional 'If you have time' area gives FOUR missing-numerator INEQUALITIES: 1/2<n/2 requires n>1;6/4>n/4 requires n<6;4/3<n/3 requires n>4;5/8>n/8 requires n<5. For the grade-3 source, use appropriate whole-number nonnegative numerators; multiple values can be correct for each. Do not impose one arbitrary numerator or count the extension as mandatory.

Why the rule works: within the SAME unit whole and fixed positive denominator, each fraction uses the SAME interval size. A larger numerator contains more equally-sized intervals, so yields a greater value. Example 3/8>2/8, but equal numerator with different denominators is a different comparison skill and must not be mixed into this lesson's assessed family.

Activity2 Spin to Win: Same Denominator is an OPEN ten-round two-player spinner game. Players distinguish their markings by different pen colors. Highest initial spin becomes Player1, who chooses round-one denominator from the ORIGINAL choices 2,3,4,6,8. Each player spins a numerator and locates the resulting fraction on the SAME line with that denominator. The greater fraction wins that round and chooses the next round denominator; after TEN rounds the participant winning more rounds wins the game. Drawn numerators and winning order vary; teacher verifies actual spinner results and equal partition geometry, not a single fixed transcript.

A valid winner check, conditional on two recorded numerators a and b and common denominator d>0, is a>b; if a=b the fractions are tied mathematically and the original source does not specify a universal tie-breaker in the public student-facing excerpt. Preserve teacher decision instead of inventing a tie rule. The original game spinner artwork and teacher-only Cool-down Same Denominator are not copied. Standalone pupil PDF, published RichV2 UI, tests, academic approval and Stage D remain unverified.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same denominator
KeyConcepts.Definition: Fractions with same positive denominator share the same unit fraction size when whole unit is the same.

KeyConcepts.Title: Improper fractions can be larger
KeyConcepts.Definition: Fraction numerator may exceed denominator; the result is beyond one whole.

KeyConcepts.Title: Incomplete inequality
KeyConcepts.Definition: Many numerator choices may meet an inequality when the denominator is fixed.
KeyConcepts.Example: n=2 or n=3 are both valid, if appropriate to task limits.

KeyConcepts.Title: Ten-round fraction game
KeyConcepts.Definition: A player's spinner result determines their fraction and position; the result cannot be a fixed source answer.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use SAME denominator for both competitors within a round; compare numerators.
KeyConcepts.Example: Conditional rolls 2 and3 on eighths:3/8 wins over2/8.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original two choose-the-greater prompts
WorkedExamples.Question: Which is greater: 1/2 or3/2; 3/8 or2/8?
Steps: 3 halves exceed 1 half, so3/2 is greater.
3 eighths exceed 2 eighths, so3/8 is greater.
With the same whole and denominator within each pair, compare the numerators: 3 > 1 and 3 > 2.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original four relation symbols
WorkedExamples.Question: Complete the four original paired comparisons.
WorkedExamples.Check: All four comparisons are strict, none equal.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original optional four missing numerators
WorkedExamples.Question: Find acceptable numerators for 1/2<n/2,6/4>n/4,4/3<n/3,5/8>n/8.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use same denominator to compare numerators.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Illustrative answers 2,5,5,4; many other valid numerators

WorkedExamples.Title: Conditional spinner round
WorkedExamples.Question: Two students choose sixths and spin numerators3 and5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Plot both on sixths line from same whole.
Steps: 3/6 at third tick,5/6 at fifth tick.
WorkedExamples.Check: Not a claim of original fixed dice/spinner outcome.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat 3/2 as invalid because it exceeds one.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original source explicitly compares 1/2 and3/2.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Compare numerator sizes across different denominators using this rule.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Different denominators mean different unit sizes.
CommonMistakes.Correction: The source activity is SAME denominator only; preserve same whole.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Provide just one accepted numerator in optional extension.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Four original prompts admit many integer solutions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check inequality truth and grade-level number domain rather than one fixed target.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Set predetermined spinner winner or invent a tie-breaker.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original game results depend on actual spinner outcomes; public student page doesn't specify tie policy.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher checks play and applies local tie handling without claiming publisher parity.

SummaryPoints: Original optional missing numerators: n>1,n<6,n>4,n<5; multiple valid responses.
Spin to Win has 10 rounds and denominator choices 2,3,4,6,8; actual spinner results teacher-reviewed.
